metadata.title: Exit times in non-Markovian drifting continuous-time random walk processes

extraction_notes.note: The paper has no theorem environments; its results are numbered equations introduced by prose ('it can be proven that', 'we find'). Each such sentence was made a claim node containing its numbered equation(s), and the preceding scenario argument a prose proof.

Classical renewal-theory and CTRW-propagator formulas restated without a name: TP1/TP2 are typed theorem (external) as cited/'well known' results stated in full, ClP20 kept a claim since it is presented as a derivation step of the example.

DP4 is one sentence introducing three symbols ($\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$, $T_b(x,r)$, $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$) and AssumP1 one sentence with three assumptions; a node cannot split a sentence, so each is kept as one node.

Worked cases with exponential/Erlang/stable distributions are long multi-paragraph examples; each was taken as one example node spanning all its numbered equations, with key claims nested inside ExP4.

Motivation, applications survey, Conclusions section, figure captions and the unnumbered inverse-Laplace eqnarray in Section 4 (kept inside ExP2) give no separate nodes; the $\varrho$ symbol is introduced inside the PP2 argument and has no definition node.

nodes.name: Continuous-time random walk with drift
nodes.statement: Thus, for $t\geqslant t_0$ we define \begin{equation} X_t=X_{t_0}+v(t-t_0)+S_{t}, \quad S_t=\sum_{n=1}^\infty J_n\ \theta(t-t_n), \end{equation} where $\theta(u)=1$ for $u \geqslant 0$, $t_n=\tau_1+\cdots+\tau_n$ are the jump times, $J_n$ the jump magnitude and $v>0$ by convention.
nodes.statement_short: CTRW with drift: $X_t$ = initial value + linear drift $vt$ + sum of jumps $J_n$ at renewal times $t_n$.

nodes.name: i.i.d. sojourn times and jumps, mutually independent
nodes.statement: All through this paper we will assume that (i) the sojourn times $\tau_n>0$ are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with probability density and cumulative distribution function (PDF and, respectively, CDF) $\psi(t)$ and $\Psi(t)= \int_0^t \psi(t')d t'$; (ii) $\{J_n\}$ is a sequence of i.i.d. random variables with common PDF $h(\cdot)$; and (iii), that $ J_m$ is independent of $\tau_n $ for any $n,m$.
nodes.statement_short: Sojourn times i.i.d. with PDF $\psi$, jumps i.i.d. with PDF $h$, and jumps independent of sojourn times.

nodes.name: Arrival (counting) process N_t
nodes.statement: In absence of drift, and when the holding times $\tau_n$ are exponentially distributed, $\tau_n\sim \mathcal E(\lambda)$ for some $\lambda >0$, the jump process $S_t$ is a classical compound Poisson process (CPP) characterized by having independent increments $S_{t+h}- S_t$; in addition the associated ``arrival-process'' $N_t\equiv\sum_{n=1}^\infty \theta(t-t_n)$ is Poisson distributed: $N_t \sim \mathcal P(\lambda t)$.
nodes.statement_short: With exponential holding times $S_t$ is a compound Poisson process and the counting process $N_t$ is Poisson.

nodes.name: Mean exit time of a drifting CTRW given only the present state
nodes.statement: Motivated by the above, here we pose the problem of evaluating the mean exit time from the interval $(0,b)$ of a drifting CTRW $X_t$ when {\it the only available information is the present state\/} $X_r=x$, where $r \geqslant 0$ is the present chronological time |note that, by adjusting the time clock and spatial scale, the results carry over to any interval $(a,b)$ and initial time $t_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Find the mean exit time from $(0,b)$ of a drifting CTRW knowing only $X_r=x$ at an arbitrary present time $r$.

nodes.name: Effect of dropping the present-is-a-jump-time assumption
nodes.statement: In particular, it remains an open question to what extent dropping the assumption that ``the present is a jump time'' affects the relevant probabilities.

nodes.name: Erlang distribution
nodes.statement: $\mathcal Er(\lambda,n)$ corresponds to having a sum of $n$ independent exponential variables and hence generalizes the exponential density in a natural way, \begin{equation} \psi(t) = \frac{\lambda^n t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} e^{-\lambda t},\, n\in \Bbb N,\, t\geqslant 0, \end{equation} while it maintains an adequate capability to fit measured data.
differentia: a sum of $n$ independent exponential variables
nodes.statement_short: Erlang$(\lambda,n)$: law of a sum of $n$ i.i.d. exponentials, with Gamma-type density.

nodes.name: Exit time quantities T_b(x,r) and mean exit time after a jump
nodes.statement: To this end let $r+\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ be the first time past $r$ at which $X_t$ exits $(0,b)$; $T_{b}(x,r)$ be its expected value: $T_{b}(x,r) =\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]$; finally let $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x) $ denote the mean exit time off $(0,b)$ after a jump $t_n$ (loosely one has $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=T_{b}(x,t_n), n=0,\dots, \infty$; however the relation between both quantities is not trivial, as we see below in Section~\ref{S_up}).
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ is the exit time from $(0,b)$ after $r$, $T_b(x,r)$ its mean, and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ the mean exit time after a jump.

nodes.name: Markov case: exit time independent of present time
nodes.statement: In the exponential Markov case $ \mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ is independent of $r$, $T_{b}(x,r)=\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ and it \it only \rm remains to formulate (and solve) the equation that this object satisfies. However this situation no longer holds in the generic, non-Markovian case where $ \mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$ does depend on $r$.

nodes.statement_short: Excess life $E_r$: time from $r$ until the next jump.

nodes.name: Proof of driftless relation
nodes.statement: Indeed let $t_{N_r}\equiv t_n$, say, be the ``last'' jump time and $E_r^- \equiv r- t_n$ the time elapsed from $t_n$ to the present. Then, with $E_r^+\equiv E_r$ one obviously has that $E_r^-+E_r^+=t_{n+1}-t_n\equiv\tau_{n+1}$, and that the exit time right after $t_n$ is that after $r$, $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$, plus $E_r^-$, and hence \begin{equation}\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=\mathbb{E} [E_r^-]+ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]=\mathbb{E}[\tau_{n+1}]-\mathbb{E}[E_r^+]+ T_{b}(x,r). \end{equation} Thus, $T_{b}(x,r) $ follows adding a correction term to $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ which depends only on $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the inter-jump time into backward and forward recurrence times and take expectations.

nodes.statement: In this section we consider the case when both drift and jumps have a positive sign, i.e. when $X_t$ is increasing.

nodes.name: Scenario argument, favorable drift
nodes.statement: Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$. If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$. Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$. Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the interval at $r+E_r$, or it does not. In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition on the excess life $l$: exit by drift if $l>\varrho$, else by the next jump or renewal from $x+vl+u$.

nodes.name: Equation relating T_b(x,r) and mean exit time after a jump (favorable drift)
nodes.statement: It can be proven that these considerations imply that $T_b(x,r)$ must satisfy |recall that $\psi(\cdot)$, $h(\cdot)$ are the waiting-time and, respectively, jump PDFs| the following equation \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r)=\left[1-\Phi\left(\varrho|r\right)\right] \varrho + \int^{\varrho}_{0} l \phi(l|r) \int^{\infty}_{b-x-v l} h(u) d ud l\nonumber \\ +\int^{\varrho}_{0} \phi(l|r) \int^{b-x-v l}_{0} h(u) \left[l+\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+vl+u\right)\right]d ud l, \end{eqnarray} an expression that relates $T_b(x,r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ satisfies an integral equation in the excess-life law $\Phi(\cdot|r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b$.

nodes.name: T_b(x,r) depends on r
nodes.statement: Note that since $\Phi\left(l|r\right)$ depends on $r$ so it does the mean time $T_b(x,r)$.

nodes.name: Explicit solvability of the favorable-drift equation
nodes.statement: It is remarkable that Eq.~(\ref{TTb_up}) \it can be solved in a fully explicit way.

nodes.name: Allied function F(y)
nodes.statement: To this end we define the allied object $\mathbb{F}(y)$, as the solution of the following integral equation \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{F}(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d l \nonumber \\ +\frac{1}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{F}\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} for $y\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbb{F}$ solves an integral equation analogous to (10), written in distance-to-boundary $y$.

nodes.name: Mean exit time equals F(b-x)
nodes.statement: Then it follows that $\mathbb{T}_b(x) =\mathbb{F}(b-x)$, for $x\in (0,b)$.

nodes.name: Closed-form Laplace transform of mean exit time after a jump
nodes.statement: We note further that taking a Laplace transformation in Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq}) we find that \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)= \frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)}{1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)}, \end{equation} where $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \mathbb{F}(y) e^{-s y}d y$, $\hat{h}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} h(u) e^{-s u}d u$, and $\hat{\psi}(s)\equiv \int^{\infty}_{0} \psi(s) e^{-s t}d t$.
nodes.statement_short: Laplace transforming (11) gives $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)$ explicitly in terms of $\hat\psi(sv)$ and $\hat h(s)$.
assumptions: taking a Laplace transformation in Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq})

nodes.name: Laplace transform of mean exit time from arbitrary present
nodes.statement: Further, we also have \begin{equation} \hat{J}(s|r) = \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)- \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v s^2\left[1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)\right]}\left[\hat{\phi}(s v|r)-\hat{\psi}(s v )\right], \end{equation} where the correction to the mean time after a jump is clearly displayed and again, for convenience, we defined $J(y|r)\equiv T_b(b-y|r)$, and extended (\ref{Tb_up}) to $y\geqslant 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\hat J(s|r)$ equals $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)$ minus an explicit correction depending on $\hat\phi(sv|r)-\hat\psi(sv)$.

nodes.name: Recovery by Laplace inversion
nodes.statement: Thus ${\mathbb{F}}(y) $ and $J(y|r)$ can be recovered by Laplace inversion, cf. Eq.~(\ref{def_m}), and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ and $T_b(x|r)$ will eventually follow.

nodes.name: Small-drift expansion
nodes.statement: Let $\mu\equiv~\mathbb{E}[\tau_{n+1}]$, $\mu_r\equiv~\mathbb{E}[E_{r}]$; then, using that $ \hat{\psi}(s v )=1-\mu sv +O(v^2)$ and so forth we see that for small $v$, $\hat{ J}(s|r)$ has an expansion in powers of $v$ as \begin{equation} \hat{J}(s|r) = \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s) - \frac{\mu-\mu_r}{s} - \frac{ \hat{h}(s) }{ 1- \hat{h}(s) } (\mu-\mu_r)\mu v + O(v^2), \end{equation} which implies, in particular, Eq.~(\ref{v=0}).
nodes.statement_short: For small $v$, $\hat J(s|r)$ expands in powers of $v$, recovering the driftless relation at order zero.
conclusions: for small $v$, $\hat{ J}(s|r)$ has an expansion in powers of $v$ as

nodes.name: Steady-state (r to infinity) solution
nodes.statement: Recalling that by the renewal theorem $\underset{t\to\infty}\lim m(t)/t = 1/\mu$, Eqs.~(\ref{hat_phi}) and~(\ref{hattime}) yield \begin{eqnarray} \hat\phi (s|\infty) &=& \frac{1-\hat \psi(s)}{s\mu}, \\ \hat{J}(s|\infty) &=& \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)- \frac{ 1- \hat{h}(s) }{v^2 s^3 \mu} \frac{1-(1+s v\mu)\hat \psi(sv)}{ 1-\hat{\psi}(s v)\hat{h}(s)}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: As $r\to\infty$ the excess-life density and $\hat J(s|\infty)$ take explicit stationary forms.

nodes.name: Exponential jumps and Erlang(2) sojourn times, favorable drift
nodes.statement: We illustrate the ideas above by detailing the case when jump magnitudes have an exponential distribution $h(u)=\gamma e^{-\gamma u}$, where $\gamma>0$ is a real parameter, and sojourn times an Erlang distribution $\tau_n\sim\mathcal Er(\lambda,2)$. Hence \begin{equation} \hat{h}(s)= \frac{\gamma}{\gamma +s},\quad \hat{\psi}(s) = \frac{\lambda^2}{(\lambda +s)^2}. \end{equation} In this case Eq.~(\ref{FF_eq}) yields that $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)$ is the following rational function \begin{equation} \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)=\frac{1}{v s^2}\frac{2\lambda \gamma v+ v(2 \lambda +\gamma v) s + v^2 s^2}{\lambda (\lambda + 2\gamma v) + v(2 \lambda +\gamma v) s+v^2 s^2}. \end{equation} Hence, the mean escape time of $(0,b)$ after a jump is \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)= \frac{2 \gamma v}{\lambda + 2 \gamma v} \varrho \nonumber\\ +\frac{\lambda^2}{z_+-z_-}\left[\frac{1-e^{-z_- \varrho}}{z_-^2}-\frac{1-e^{-z_+ \varrho}}{z_+^2}\right], \end{eqnarray} where we recall that $v \varrho=b-x$ is the initial distance to the boundary $b$ and \begin{equation} z_{\pm}\equiv \lambda +\frac{\gamma v}{2}\left(1\pm\sqrt{1-\frac{4\lambda}{\gamma v}}\right), \end{equation} with $\mbox{Re}[z_{\pm}]>0$. The evaluation of the mean exit time starting at $r$, $T_b(x,r)$, involves the renewal function and excess-life distribution. We first obtain from Eq.~(\ref{hat_phi}) \begin{equation} \hat m(s)=\frac{\lambda^2}{s^2(2\lambda +s)}, \quad \hat \phi(s|r)=\hat \psi(s)+ \frac{ (1-e^{-2 \lambda r})s\lambda }{ 2 (\lambda +s)^2}. \end{equation} By inversion we get $m(t)= \big(2 \lambda t + e^{-2 \lambda t}-1\big)/4$ and \begin{equation} \ \Phi(t|r) = 1-e^{-\lambda t} \left[ 1+ \left(\frac{ 1+{e^{-2 \lambda r }}}{2}\right)\lambda t \right]. \end{equation} Then by using Eq.~(\ref{hattime}) we find at last that \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r) =\mathbb{T}_b(x) \nonumber \\ - \frac{\lambda}{2}\frac{1-e^{-2\lambda r}}{z_+-z_-}\left[\frac{1-e^{-z_- \varrho}}{z_-}-\frac{1-e^{-z_+ \varrho}}{z_+}\right]. \end{eqnarray} Plots of this function in terms of $x$ are given in Fig.~\ref{E2_up} for several values of $r$ and a certain choice of the rest of parameters. \begin{figure}[htb] { \includegraphics[width=0.45\textwidth,keepaspectratio=true]{Fig1.eps} } \caption{(Color online) Sample representations of $T_b(x,r)$ for different values of $r$: $r=0$, i.e. $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$, solid (black) line, $r=0.4$, dashed (red) line and $r=10.0$, dot-dashed (blue) line. The rest of the parameters were chosen as follows: $b=1.0$, $v=0.1$, $\lambda=1.0$ and $\gamma=0.1$.} \end{figure} Finally note how, in particular, if $v=0$ then \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)=\frac{2}{\lambda}\left[1+\gamma (b-x)\right] &=& \mathbb{E}[\tau_n] \left(1+ \frac{b-x}{\mathbb{E}[J_n]}\right), \\ T_{b}(x,r)&=&\mathbb{T}_b(x) -\frac{1- e^{-2\lambda r}}{2\lambda}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$, renewal function, excess-life CDF and $T_b(x,r)$ for exponential jumps and Erlang(2) waiting times.

nodes.name: Drift and jumps of opposite sign
nodes.statement: We now consider the case when the sign of the drift $vt>0$ is opposite to that of the jumps.
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps

nodes.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
nodes.statement: The resulting process is a prototype model in risk management to describe the dynamics of the cahsflow $X_t$ at an insurance company under the assumption that premiums are received at a constant rate $v>0$ and that the company incurs in losses $J_n<0$ from claims reported at times $t_n, n=1,\dots\infty$ (the Cramer-Lundberg model).
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps
nodes.statement_short: Insurance cash flow with constant premium rate $v$ and claim losses $J_n<0$ at times $t_n$.

nodes.name: Scenario argument, opposite drift
nodes.statement: As before, we analyze the evolution starting at $t=r$ with $X_r=x$. Then if $E_r=l$, $l > \varrho$, the drift will drive the process out of the region through the {\it upper boundary\/} at time $r+\varrho$. Otherwise ($l \leqslant \varrho$) at least a jump $J_{N_r+1}=-u$, say, occurs at time $t_{N_r+1}$ before escape, and two possible scenarios appear depending on the relative magnitudes of the jump size and the location of the process right before the jump, $X_t=x+v l$: for $u\geqslant x+v l$ the process will leave the interval through the {\it lower boundary\/} at $r+E_r$, but when $u<x+v l$ the process after the jump will remain inside the interval, $X_{r+l}=x+v l-u$, the exit problem will start afresh, and the mean escape time will be increased by $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v l-u\right)$.

nodes.statement_short: Condition on the excess life: upper exit by drift, lower exit by a large jump, or renewal from $x+vl-u$.

nodes.statement: Unfortunately, unlike what happens for the case considered in the previous Section, Eq.~(\ref{TTb_down}) can not be solved in closed form for arbitrary PDFs $\psi(\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$.

nodes.name: Integro-differential equation for Erlang(2) times
nodes.statement: Indeed, in this case (\ref{TTb_down}) reads \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)= \frac{2-\left(2+\lambda \varrho\right)e^{-\lambda \varrho}}{\lambda} \nonumber \\+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2} \int^{b}_{x} \left(z-x\right)e^{-\lambda \left(z-x\right)/v} \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} and hence, by differentiation we find that $ \mathbb{T}_b(x)$, for $0< x< b$, also satisfies the following integral-differential equation: \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b''(x)-\frac{2\lambda}{v}\mathbb{T}_b'(x)+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2}\mathbb{T}_b(x)= \frac{2\lambda}{v^2} \nonumber \\+\frac{\lambda^2}{v^2}\int^{x}_{0}h(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(x-u\right)d u, \end{eqnarray} subject to the following boundary conditions: \begin{equation} \lim_{x\to b}\mathbb{T}_b(x)=0,\mbox{ and }\lim_{x\to b}\mathbb{T}_b'(x)=-1/v. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Laplace-transform solution with unknown constants A, B
nodes.statement: We first consider a general solution to this equation extending it to the full real axis, so we will drop the subscript in $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$. We find a solution by Laplace transformation as \begin{eqnarray} \hat{ \mathbb{T} }(s)= \frac{2\lambda/s + (B v-2 \lambda A)v + A v^2s}{\lambda^2[1-\hat{h}(s)]-2\lambda v s+ v^2s^2}, \end{eqnarray} where $A $ and $B$ are $\mathbb{T}(0)$ and $\mathbb{T}'(0)$ respectively.
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps
nodes.statement_short: Extending to the real axis, Laplace transform gives $\hat{\mathbb{T}}(s)$ in terms of $A=\mathbb{T}(0)$, $B=\mathbb{T}'(0)$.

nodes.name: Boundary conditions fix A and B
nodes.statement: By inversion, cf. Eq.~(\ref{def_m}), $\mathbb{T}(x)$ follows in terms of $A$ and $B$. By requiring~(\ref{boundary}) we obtain a linear algebraic system for $A$ and $B$, which upon solution yields $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ in closed form.

nodes.name: b to infinity limit and ruin
nodes.statement: The limit $b\to \infty$ is interesting as $\mathbb{T}_\infty(x)$ gives the probability that $X_t$ ever hits $0$. This corresponds to the classical ruin probability in an insurance context. It turns out that $\mathbb{T}_\infty(x)$ can be determined in a direct way that avoids solving the aforementioned linear system.
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps

nodes.name: Mean exit time in the b to infinity limit
nodes.statement: Without proof~\footnote{We elaborate on a similar expression in the next section.} we note that if $\lambda > 2 \gamma v $ then \begin{equation} \mathbb{T}_\infty(x)=\frac{2(1+\gamma x)}{\lambda-2 \gamma v}= \left( 1+\gamma x \right)\Big/\left( \frac{1}{ \Bbb E[\tau_n]}- \frac{v}{ \Bbb E[J_n]} \right), \end{equation} while $\mathbb{T}_\infty(x)=\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda>2\gamma v$, $\mathbb{T}_\infty(x)=2(1+\gamma x)/(\lambda-2\gamma v)$; otherwise infinite.

nodes.name: Two-sided jumps
nodes.statement: We finally consider the general case corresponding to a jump process where $J_n$ can take both signs and hence can exit $(0,b)$ through either of the boundaries.

nodes.name: Scenario argument, two-sided jumps
nodes.statement: The relevant analysis is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates the possibility of an upper exit due to a jump: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary. If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process. When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.
nodes.statement_short: Same excess-life conditioning as before, adding the possibility of an upper exit by a jump.

nodes.name: Equations for exit times, two-sided jumps
nodes.statement: Skipping minor details we obtain that $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ and $T_b(x,r)$ satisfy respectively \begin{eqnarray} T_b(x,r)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Phi\left(l|r\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \phi\left(\left.\frac{z-x}{v}\right|r\right) \int^{b-z}_{-z} h(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(z+u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} and \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi\left(l\right)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{1}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \psi\left(\frac{z-x}{v}\right) \int^{b-z}_{-z} h(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(z+u\right)dud z. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $T_b(x,r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ satisfy integral equations (35)-(36) with jumps of both signs.

nodes.name: No closed form in general, two-sided
nodes.statement: In a general situation, the latter integral equation is not solvable in closed form.

nodes.name: Decomposition of jump PDF by sign
nodes.statement: To gain some insight we use the decomposition $ h(x)= q h_+(x) + p h_-(x)$ where $p$ is the probability that a given jump be negative, $q\equiv 1-p$ and $h_{\pm}(\cdot)$ are the jump PDF in the positive/negative regions, i.e. $h_+(x)\equiv h(x) \theta(x) \big/ q$, say.
nodes.statement_short: Split $h=qh_++ph_-$ with $p$ the probability of a negative jump.

nodes.name: Recovering the favorable-drift case
nodes.statement: Note that if $h_-(x)=0, \forall x\leqslant 0$, we recover the case considered in Section~\ref{S_up}, solvable via Laplace transformation.

nodes.name: Closed solution when h_- vanishes on (-b,0)
nodes.statement: It turns out that we can still \it construct an analytic closed solution \rm in the more general case when $h_-(x) $ vanishes \it only \rm on $(-b,0)$ |but not on $(-\infty,-b]$.

nodes.name: Integral equation with q factor
nodes.statement: The equation for $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ reads in this case \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)= \int^{\varrho}_{0}\left[1-\Psi\left(l\right)\right]d l \nonumber\\+ \frac{q}{v}\int^{b}_{x} \psi\left(\frac{z-x}{v}\right) \int^{b-z}_{0} h_+(u) \mathbb{T}_b\left(z+u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} while a similar expression, with $\phi(\cdot|r)$ in place of $\psi(\cdot)$, holds for $T_b(x,r)$.

nodes.name: Reduction to the favorable-drift technique
nodes.statement: Note that these equations are independent of the form of $h_-(\cdot)$ and apart from the factor $q$ in front of the second term they resemble Eqs.~(\ref{Tb_up}) and~(\ref{TTb_up}); it follows that we can resort to the same technique used in Section~\ref{S_up}: We consider \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{F}(y)= \int^{y/v}_{0}\left[1-\Psi(l)\right]d l \nonumber \\+ \frac{q}{v}\int^{y}_{0} \psi\left(\frac{y-z}{v}\right) \int^{z}_{0} h(u) \mathbb{F}\left(z-u\right)d ud z, \end{eqnarray} for $y\in \mathbb{R}^{+}$ which is again solvable by means of a Laplace transform; then $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ follows from $\mathbb{T}_b(x) =\mathbb{F}(b-x)$ for $x\in (0,b)$.
nodes.statement_short: With $h_-$ supported below $-b$ the equations mimic (9)-(10) up to factor $q$, solvable by Laplace transform via $\mathbb{F}$.

nodes.name: Erlang(2) times and exponential jumps, two-sided case
nodes.statement: With the previous selection for $h(\cdot)$ and $\psi(\cdot)$, Eq.~(\ref{h_hat}), and in terms of $z=sv $ we find \begin{eqnarray} \hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)=\frac{v}{z} \frac{2\lambda \gamma v + (2 \lambda+\gamma v ) z + z^2}{p \lambda^2 \gamma v + \lambda (\lambda +2\gamma v ) z+ (2 \lambda +\gamma v ) z^2+z^3 }. \end{eqnarray} We first consider the case when $\lambda =\gamma v$. Under this assumption $\hat{\mathbb{F}}(s)$ has poles at $z=z_j\equiv \lambda \left(q^{1/3} e^{2\pi ij/3}-1\right)$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, and $z=0$. Inverse Laplace transformation yields the mean exit time as \begin{equation} \mathbb{T}_b(x)= \frac{2}{ p\lambda}+ \sum_{j=1}^3 \frac{ 1+q^{-1/3} e^{-2\pi ij/3}}{ 3 z_j} e^{z_j\varrho}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit $\hat{\mathbb{F}}$ for the two-sided case, inverted in closed form when $\lambda=\gamma v$.

nodes.name: Roots have negative real parts
nodes.statement: To this end we note that by appealing to Hurwitz's stability criteria it can be proven that all three roots $z_j$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, of the denominator in expression (\ref{FF}) |apart from $z=0$| have negative real parts.
conclusions: all three roots $z_j$, $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, of the denominator  in  expression (\ref{FF}) |apart from $z=0$|  have negative real parts

nodes.name: Residue form of mean exit time
nodes.statement: Hence, evaluating the inversion integral by residues we find \begin{eqnarray} \mathbb{T}_b(x)=\frac{2}{ p\lambda} + \sum_{j=1}^3C_j e^{z_j\varrho}, \end{eqnarray} where $C_j$ are certain constants.

nodes.name: Large-b limit of mean exit time
nodes.statement: Thus, letting $b\to\infty$ we see that $\mathbb{T}_b(x) \underset{b \to\infty}\to \frac{2 }{ p\lambda} =\frac{\mathbb{E}[\tau_n]}{1-\mathbb{E}[\theta(J_n)]}$.
nodes.statement_short: As $b\to\infty$ the mean exit time tends to $2/(p\lambda)=\mathbb{E}[\tau_n]/(1-\mathbb{E}[\theta(J_n)])$.

nodes.name: Correction to T_b(x,r), two-sided case
nodes.statement: The evaluation of the correction to $T_b(x,r)$ does not present particular difficulties. We leave it as an exercise to the interested reader.

nodes.name: Continuum limit erases the r-dependence
nodes.statement: The major drawback within our set-up is that as $\mu \to 0$ the variable $r$, the time elapsed from the last known jump, tends to zero as well, and the distinction between $T_b(x,r)$ and $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ becomes irrelevant.

nodes.name: Backward/forward recurrence decomposition
nodes.statement: Indeed let $t_{N_r}\equiv t_n$, say, be the ``last'' jump time and $E_r^- \equiv r- t_n$ the time elapsed from $t_n$ to the present. Then, with $E_r^+\equiv E_r$ one obviously has that $E_r^-+E_r^+=t_{n+1}-t_n\equiv\tau_{n+1}$, and that the exit time right after $t_n$ is that after $r$, $\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}$, plus $E_r^-$, and hence \begin{equation}\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)=\mathbb{E} [E_r^-]+ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{t}_b^{x,r}]=\mathbb{E}[\tau_{n+1}]-\mathbb{E}[E_r^+]+ T_{b}(x,r). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce last jump and backward time; exit after $t_n$ equals exit after $r$ plus $E_r^-$, take expectations.

nodes.name: Correction depends only on r
nodes.statement: Thus, $T_{b}(x,r) $ follows adding a correction term to $\mathbb{T}_{b}(x)$ which depends only on $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $T_b(x,r)$ is $\mathbb{T}_b(x)$ plus an $r$-only correction.

nodes.name: Exit by drift before next jump
nodes.statement: Let us assume that at time $t=r$ the system is in $X_r=x\in(0,b)$, and that the excess life $E_r$ is known in advance, $E_r=l$. If the excess life is longer than $\varrho \equiv {b-x\over v}< l$, the drift will drive the process out of the region at time $r+\varrho$, before the next jump takes place at $t_{N_r+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Given excess life $l>\varrho$, the drift drives the process out at $r+\varrho$.

nodes.name: A jump occurs before exit
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $l \leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump of size $J_{N_r+1}=u$ will occur prior to exiting the interval. Note that just before $t_{N_r+1}$ the process $X_t$ is no longer at $x$, but at $x+v l$. Therefore, two possible scenarios appear: either the jump size is larger than the remaining distance up to the upper boundary, $u\geqslant b-x-v l$, and the process leaves the interval at $r+E_r$, or it does not. In the latter case the problem renews from $t=r+l$, $X_{r+l}=x+v l+u$, so the mean escape time will be increased by an amount $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v l+u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: If $l\le\varrho$ the next jump either exits or the problem renews from $x+vl+u$.

nodes.name: Upper exit by drift
nodes.statement: As before, we analyze the evolution starting at $t=r$ with $X_r=x$. Then if $E_r=l$, $l > \varrho$, the drift will drive the process out of the region through the {\it upper boundary\/} at time $r+\varrho$.
nodes.statement_short: If $l>\varrho$ the drift drives the process through the upper boundary.

nodes.name: Jump before escape
nodes.statement: Otherwise ($l \leqslant \varrho$) at least a jump $J_{N_r+1}=-u$, say, occurs at time $t_{N_r+1}$ before escape, and two possible scenarios appear depending on the relative magnitudes of the jump size and the location of the process right before the jump, $X_t=x+v l$: for $u\geqslant x+v l$ the process will leave the interval through the {\it lower boundary\/} at $r+E_r$, but when $u<x+v l$ the process after the jump will remain inside the interval, $X_{r+l}=x+v l-u$, the exit problem will start afresh, and the mean escape time will be increased by $\mathbb{T}_b\left(x+v l-u\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise a downward jump either exits through 0 or the problem restarts from $x+vl-u$.
nodes.section: 4 The case of opposite drift and jumps

nodes.name: Upper exit by drift
nodes.statement: The relevant analysis is similar to that of the last section if one incorporates the possibility of an upper exit due to a jump: If $E_r=l>\varrho$ the drift drives directly the process through the upper boundary.
nodes.statement_short: Same analysis as before; if $l>\varrho$ the drift drives the process out.

nodes.name: Jump before exit, both signs
nodes.statement: If $l\leqslant \varrho$ at least a jump occurs before the exit of the process. When the size $u$ of this jump is positive and $u\geqslant b-x-vl$ the process leaves the interval at time $r+E_r$ through the upper boundary, when $u\leqslant -(x+vl)<0$ the exit takes place through the lower boundary, otherwise the process remains inside the interval $(0,b)$ and the problem restarts.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise a jump exits upward, downward, or restarts the problem inside $(0,b)$.
